questions.clue: A rule that converts a sample into a value for an unknown population quantity.
questions.explanation: An estimator is the rule applied to the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimator

questions.clue: The specific numerical result obtained after applying a rule to the observed data.
questions.explanation: An estimate is the result of applying an estimator to one sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimate

questions.clue: A range calculated from sample data by a method with a stated long-run success rate for containing the target parameter.
questions.explanation: The confidence rate describes the repeated-sampling behavior of the interval procedure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: The stated long-run capture rate of an interval procedure under its model assumptions.
questions.explanation: For a valid 95% procedure, about 95% of repeated intervals capture the fixed target.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue: The reference claim evaluated by a significance test, often expressing no difference.
questions.explanation: The test assesses how unusual the evidence is under this reference claim.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 307, Null hypothesis

questions.clue: The claim that specifies how the population could differ from the test’s reference claim.
questions.explanation: The alternative determines which directions or values count against the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Alternative hypothesis

questions.clue: Researchers record patients’ existing diets and follow their health without choosing diets for them.
questions.explanation: The researchers observe existing exposures without assigning them.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 308, Observational study

questions.clue: A coin toss determines which treatment each participant receives.
questions.explanation: Chance assigns treatment to enrolled participants.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random allocation

questions.clue: People receive a pill but are kept unaware of whether it contains the study drug.
questions.explanation: Hiding treatment identity from participants limits expectation effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 57, Blinding

questions.clue: A comparison pill looks just like the study drug but contains none of its active ingredient.
questions.explanation: A placebo mimics treatment without including its active component.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Placebo

questions.clue: One survey measures employment and current health during the same interview, with no follow-up.
questions.explanation: Exposure and outcome information are measured at one time in a cross-sectional study.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Cross-sectional study

questions.clue: Researchers group people by a recorded exposure and follow both groups for new cases of illness.
questions.explanation: A cohort study follows a defined group to observe outcomes over time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 90, Cohort study

questions.clue:
c × SE
where a symmetric interval is estimate ± c × SE
questions.explanation: In a symmetric interval, the multiplier times the standard error is the half-width.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$c\times\mathrm{SE}$
where a symmetric interval is $\mathrm{estimate}\pm c\times\mathrm{SE}$

questions.clue:
x̄ − c × SE
for a symmetric interval with c > 0
questions.explanation: Subtracting the margin of error gives the lower endpoint.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$\bar x-c\times\mathrm{SE}$
for a symmetric interval with $c > 0$

questions.clue:
x̄ + c × SE
for a symmetric interval with c > 0
questions.explanation: Adding the margin of error gives the upper endpoint.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$\bar x+c\times\mathrm{SE}$
for a symmetric interval with $c > 0$

questions.clue:
s / √n
for the mean of n independent observations with sample SD s
questions.explanation: Replacing the population standard deviation with s estimates the standard error of the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$
for the mean of $n$ independent observations with sample SD $s$
questions.math_explanation: Replacing the population standard deviation with $s$ estimates the standard error of the mean.

questions.clue:
2c × SE
for a symmetric interval x̄ ± c × SE
questions.explanation: The upper and lower limits each lie one margin of error from the center, so the total width is twice the margin.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$2c\times\mathrm{SE}$
for a symmetric interval $\bar{x}\pm c\times\mathrm{SE}$

questions.clue:
P(reject H₀ given H₀ is true)
for a simple null hypothesis
questions.explanation: This is the probability of making a Type I error, rejecting a true null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error
questions.math_clue:
$P(\mathrm{reject}\ H_0\mid H_0\ \mathrm{is\ true})$
for a simple null hypothesis

questions.clue: The difference between an estimator’s average over repeated samples and its target parameter.
questions.explanation: Bias measures systematic departure in the estimator’s long-run average.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 45, Bias

questions.clue: An estimator becomes arbitrarily close to its target with probability approaching one as sample size grows.
questions.explanation: Consistency describes accuracy in probability as the sample grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Consistency

questions.clue: A comparison of how much two unbiased estimators of the same parameter vary over repeated samples.
questions.explanation: Among unbiased estimators for one target, the smaller-variance estimator is more efficient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 149, Efficiency

questions.clue: Under the null model, the chance of a test result at least as extreme as the observed result.
questions.explanation: Extremeness is measured by the chosen test in the direction or directions specified by its alternative.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 346, P-value

questions.clue: At a specified alternative, the long-run probability of rejecting the null hypothesis.
questions.explanation: Power is the probability of detecting the specified departure from the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: The set of test statistic values that trigger rejection of the reference claim.
questions.explanation: The decision rule rejects the null if the statistic lands in this set.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 115, Critical region

questions.clue: Researchers start with people with and without a disease, then compare past exposure between the two groups.
questions.explanation: Selection starts with disease status, and the study compares earlier exposures.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 69, Case-control study

questions.clue: Each participant receives both treatments in different periods, with treatment order assigned by chance.
questions.explanation: Each person receives more than one treatment in different periods.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Crossover design

questions.clue: Researchers match one treated patient with one untreated patient of similar age, then compare within each pair.
questions.explanation: Pairing links comparable observations for a within-pair comparison.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 271, Matched pairs

questions.clue: Plots are grouped by soil type, then treatments are randomly assigned within each soil group.
questions.explanation: Blocking builds known plot differences into the design before treatment is assigned.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: A trial assigns every combination of two temperatures and three processing speeds.
questions.explanation: A factorial experiment combines levels of two or more factors to study their effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Neither study participants nor the people who measure their outcomes are told which treatment was assigned.
questions.explanation: Both specified groups are kept unaware of treatment identity.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Double-blind
questions.convention: Names the two masked groups because practices vary between trials.

questions.clue: The treatment group is younger, and age itself affects the outcome. What threatens a causal interpretation?
questions.explanation: Age is associated with treatment and also affects outcome, so the treatment comparison mixes the effects.
questions.reference: UC Berkeley STAT 2, Fall 2024, Module 1, Data collection and variables: https://stat2.berkeley.edu/fall-2024/

questions.clue: Researchers test for a decrease in wait time. An increase provides no evidence for their specified alternative.
questions.explanation: This test’s alternative specifies just one direction of departure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 311, One-sided test

questions.clue:
E[(θ̂ − θ)²]
where θ̂ estimates the fixed target θ
questions.explanation: The mean squared error averages the squared difference between estimator and target.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squared error
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{E}[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2]$
where $\hat{\theta}$ estimates the fixed target $\theta$

questions.clue:
Set x̄ = Eθ[X] and solve for θ.
Assume one unknown parameter.
questions.explanation: The method equates a sample moment to the corresponding population moment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 277, Method of moments
questions.math_clue:
$\bar x=\mathrm{E}_{\theta}[X]$
Match the sample mean to the model expectation and solve for $\theta$. Assume one unknown parameter.

questions.clue:
The value of θ that maximizes L(θ)
for the observed data.
questions.explanation: The maximizing parameter value is the maximum likelihood estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 273, Maximum likelihood estimation
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{arg}\,\max_{\theta}\,L(\theta)$
Choose the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood for the observed data.

questions.clue:
(x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n)
for a hypothesized mean μ₀ and sample SD s
questions.explanation: The one-sample t statistic uses an estimated standard error for a single sample mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student’s t-distribution
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$
for a hypothesized mean $\mu_0$ and sample SD $s$
questions.math_explanation: The one-sample $t$ statistic uses an estimated standard error for a single sample mean.

questions.clue: P(do not reject H₀ given a specified alternative is true)
questions.explanation: This is the probability of making a Type II error at the specified alternative.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type II error
questions.math_clue:
$P(\mathrm{fail\ to\ reject}\ H_0\mid H_1)$
Here $H_1$ denotes a specified true alternative.

questions.clue:
(x̄ − μ₀) / (σ / √n)
for known population SD σ and hypothesized mean μ₀
questions.explanation: The z statistic uses the known population standard deviation in its standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 468, z-test
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$
for known population SD $\sigma$ and hypothesized mean $\mu_0$

questions.clue:
The number c satisfying P(Z > c) = α
when Z follows its null distribution.
questions.explanation: The critical value is the cutoff for the test statistic.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 115, Critical value
questions.math_clue:
$P(Z>c)=\alpha$
What is the number $c$ that satisfies this condition when $Z$ follows its null distribution?

questions.clue: Keep all values θ₀ for which the matching two-sided test of H₀: θ = θ₀ does not reject at level α.
questions.explanation: Inverting a family of tests gives a confidence set from the null values not rejected.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 415, Lesson 10, confidence interval and hypothesis test duality: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/Lesson10
questions.math_clue:
$H_0:\theta=\theta_0$
Keep all values $\theta_0$ for which the matching two-sided test of this null does not reject at level $\alpha$.

questions.clue: The population quantity a study is trying to estimate, before choosing an analysis rule.
questions.explanation: The estimand defines the target, such as a population mean difference.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimand

questions.clue: A rule whose expected value exactly equals the target parameter at every parameter value in the model.
questions.explanation: Across repeated samples at a fixed parameter, the average result equals that parameter.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 440, Unbiased

questions.clue: A summary that retains all the sample’s information about the parameter under the specified model.
questions.explanation: Given this statistic, the conditional distribution of the data contains no further dependence on the parameter.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 420, Sufficient statistic

questions.clue: Estimate an unknown function of a parameter by substituting a sample estimate for that parameter.
questions.explanation: The unknown parameter is replaced by its estimate inside the function.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Plug-in principle

questions.clue: Each volunteer stays on the one treatment they were assigned for the full follow-up.
questions.explanation: Separate treatment groups are followed at the same time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 316, Parallel groups design

questions.clue: A clinic describes six patients with an unusual condition, without a separate comparison group.
questions.explanation: A case series describes multiple cases without a comparator group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Case series

questions.clue: Old employment files identify groups with different past exposures. Later disease records already exist for both groups.
questions.explanation: The groups are defined by exposure, and historical records provide outcomes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 370, Retrospective cohort study

questions.clue: A crossover trial leaves a treatment-free gap between periods so the first treatment can wear off.
questions.explanation: The gap reduces the chance that the previous treatment affects the next period.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 453, Wash-out period

questions.clue:
x̄ ± c × s/√n
where c comes from a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: The t multiplier and sample standard deviation produce an interval for one population mean.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT Online, S.2 Confidence Intervals, t-interval and equal-tail multipliers: https://online.stat.psu.edu/statprogram/reviews/statistical-concepts/confidence-intervals
questions.math_clue:
$\bar x\pm c\times\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$
where $c$ comes from a $t$ distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom
questions.math_explanation: The $t$ multiplier and sample standard deviation produce an interval for one population mean.

questions.clue:
x̄ ± c × σ/√n
where σ is known and c is a standard normal cutoff
questions.explanation: With known population standard deviation, a normal cutoff sets the confidence interval’s margin.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 415, Lesson 6, Theorem 6.1, Z-Interval for a Mean: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/Lesson06
questions.math_clue:
$\bar x\pm c\times\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$
where $\sigma$ is known and $c$ is a standard normal cutoff

questions.concept: estimated standard error of a proportion
questions.clue:
√[p̂(1 − p̂) / n]
for an observed proportion p̂ and n independent trials
choices: Estimated standard error of a proportion
Standard error under a specified null
questions.answer: Estimated standard error of a proportion
questions.explanation: The sample proportion substitutes for the unknown population probability in the standard error.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 8, §8.1 Inference for One Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson08
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}$
for an observed proportion $\hat{p}$ and $n$ independent trials

questions.clue:
Σᵢ (xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)
for n > 1 independent draws with a common finite variance
questions.explanation: With the n − 1 correction, the estimator’s expectation equals the population variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}{n-1}$
for $n > 1$ independent draws with a common finite variance
questions.math_explanation: With the $n-1$ correction, the estimator’s expectation equals the population variance.

questions.clue: A range designed to contain a new individual observation at a stated long-run rate.
questions.explanation: Predicting an individual includes variation of the new observation itself.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 462, §4.11 Prediction Interval for a New Response: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat462/node/127/

questions.clue: A range intended to contain at least a chosen fraction of the population with a stated confidence level.
questions.explanation: The target is a fraction of the population, such as at least 90% of individual values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 432, Tolerance interval

questions.clue: A significance test whose alternative allows a population mean to differ from its reference in either direction.
questions.explanation: Departures above and below the null value can provide evidence against the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 438, Two-sided test

questions.clue: A difference is large enough to matter in its real-world setting, even before considering its p-value.
questions.explanation: Practical relevance depends on the size and consequences of the effect.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 6, Hypothesis Testing Part 2, Practical Significance: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson06

questions.clue: The extent to which an estimator gives similar values across repeated samples.
questions.explanation: A smaller sampling standard deviation indicates greater precision.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 335, Precision

questions.clue: A quantitative measure of how large a group difference or association is.
questions.explanation: An effect size expresses magnitude, such as a mean difference in original or standardized units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 148, Effect size

questions.clue: A trial finds a treatment effect and rejects no effect, but in truth the treatments are equally effective.
questions.explanation: The test rejected a true null hypothesis.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error

questions.clue: A test fails to detect a real treatment effect and leaves the no-effect hypothesis unrejected.
questions.explanation: The test failed to reject a false null hypothesis.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type II error

questions.clue: A trial analyzes patients under their originally assigned groups, even when some switch treatments.
questions.explanation: Keeping original groups preserves the randomized comparison for the assignment strategy.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Intention-to-treat analysis

questions.clue: A recruiter confirms eligibility and enrolls a participant before a central service reveals the upcoming assignment.
questions.explanation: Concealing upcoming assignments prevents foreknowledge from influencing who is enrolled.
questions.reference: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, v5.1, Chapter 8, allocation concealment: https://training.cochrane.org/sites/training.cochrane.org/files/public/uploads/resources/Handbook5_1/Chapter_8_Handbook_5_2_8.pdf

questions.clue: Some volunteers report relief after an inert pill because they expected it to help.
questions.explanation: Expectations can affect outcomes even if the pill lacks an active ingredient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Placebo effect

questions.clue: One treatment is a pill and the other an injection. Each group receives its active treatment and the other route’s look-alike placebo.
questions.explanation: The paired delivery routes make treatment identity harder to infer.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Double-dummy technique

questions.clue:
p₁ − p₂
where p₁ and p₂ are two groups’ event probabilities
questions.explanation: Subtracting the risks gives the absolute difference on the probability scale.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 3, Two-Way Tables and Relative Risk: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson03
questions.math_clue:
$p_1-p_2$
where $p_1$ and $p_2$ are two groups’ event probabilities

questions.clue:
p₁ / p₂
where p₁ and p₂ are group risks and p₂ > 0
questions.explanation: Dividing the probabilities gives risk in group one relative to group two.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 3, Two-Way Tables and Relative Risk: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson03
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{p_1}{p_2}$
where $p_1$ and $p_2$ are group risks and $p_2>0$

questions.clue:
[p₁/(1 − p₁)] / [p₂/(1 − p₂)]
for group probabilities strictly between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Convert each probability to odds, then divide the two odds.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds ratio
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_2/(1-p_2)}$
for group probabilities strictly between 0 and 1

questions.clue:
α/2
for each of the two equally sized tails outside the central area 1 − α
questions.explanation: The two tails share the total probability α evenly.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT Online, S.2 Confidence Intervals, t-interval and equal-tail multipliers: https://online.stat.psu.edu/statprogram/reviews/statistical-concepts/confidence-intervals
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\alpha}{2}$
for each of the two equally sized tails outside the central area $1-\alpha$
questions.math_explanation: The two tails share the total probability $\alpha$ evenly.

questions.clue:
(x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)
for independent means and a null difference of zero
questions.explanation: Welch’s standard error uses the two separate sample variances.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 555, §2.6, t-tests, Welch’s two-sample t statistic: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat555/node/36/
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}$
for independent means and a null difference of zero

questions.clue:
1 − β
where β is the probability of missing a fixed real effect
questions.explanation: The chance of detecting the fixed effect is one minus the chance of missing it.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power
questions.math_clue:
$1-\beta$
where $\beta$ is the probability of missing a fixed real effect

questions.clue: The probability of making one or more false rejections across a family of tests.
questions.explanation: The event is at least one rejected true null in the entire family.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 164, Familywise error rate

questions.clue: A treatment administered earlier continues to influence outcomes during the next treatment period.
questions.explanation: Residual effects from the earlier treatment contaminate the later period.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 69, Carryover effects

questions.clue: A trial comparison restricted to participants meeting predefined adherence requirements.
questions.explanation: Restriction by adherence can change the comparability initially provided by random assignment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Per protocol

questions.clue: An estimate is recalculated repeatedly, leaving out a different single observation each time.
questions.explanation: Leave-one-out estimates can be combined to assess bias or standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 226, Jackknife

questions.clue: Under an exchangeable no-group-effect model, shuffle group labels many times and compare the observed mean difference with the shuffled differences.
questions.explanation: Shuffling labels builds a reference distribution under the null model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Permutation test

questions.clue: For paired measurements with no ties, a researcher counts increases and compares the count with a fair-binomial reference.
questions.explanation: The sign test uses directions of change without their magnitudes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 393, Sign test

questions.clue: Participants know their treatments, but the reviewer scoring their scans sees anonymized IDs without group labels.
questions.explanation: Keeping assessors unaware can reduce differences in judgment across groups.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 57, Blinding

questions.clue: A factory needs an upper limit for its mean defect concentration at a chosen confidence level, with no lower endpoint.
questions.explanation: This procedure limits the parameter from above while allowing all smaller values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue:
(x₁ + x₂) / (n₁ + n₂)
for independent success counts x₁ and x₂ with a shared probability
questions.explanation: Add all successes and divide by the combined number of trials.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 9, Inference for Two Samples: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson09
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}$
for independent success counts $x_1$ and $x_2$ with a shared probability

questions.clue:
d̄ ± c × s_d/√n
where c is a t cutoff and d is the within-pair difference
questions.explanation: Use one observation per pair, namely its difference.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 7, Comparing Two Population Parameters: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson07
questions.math_clue:
$\bar d\pm c\times\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}$
where $c$ is a $t$ cutoff and $d$ is the within-pair difference

questions.clue:
α/m
used as each local cutoff when testing m hypotheses to control familywise error
questions.explanation: The sum of the local Type I error bounds is at most α.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bonferroni correction
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\alpha}{m}$
used as each local cutoff when testing $m$ hypotheses to control familywise error
questions.math_explanation: The sum of the local Type I error bounds is at most $\alpha$.

questions.clue:
(p̂ − p₀) / √[p₀(1 − p₀)/n]
for a sample proportion p̂ and hypothesized p₀
questions.explanation: The denominator uses the null probability p₀ in the standard error.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 8, §8.1 Inference for One Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson08
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$
for a sample proportion $\hat{p}$ and hypothesized $p_0$
questions.math_explanation: The denominator uses the null probability $p_0$ in the standard error.

questions.clue: MSE of θ̂ = Var(θ̂) + [E(θ̂) − θ]²
questions.explanation: Expanding squared error shows variance and squared bias add to total mean squared error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squared error
questions.math_clue: $\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})+[\mathrm{E}(\hat{\theta})-\theta]^2$

questions.clue:
√[p̂₁(1 − p̂₁)/n₁ + p̂₂(1 − p̂₂)/n₂]
for two independent sample proportions
questions.explanation: Estimate each group’s variance separately when constructing the usual interval for their difference.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 9, Inference for Two Samples: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson09
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$
for two independent sample proportions

questions.clue: A measurement rule overestimates its target on average across repeated samples. How should its bias be described?
questions.explanation: Bias is positive when the estimator's expectation exceeds its target.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 45, Bias

questions.clue: An estimator has a systematic offset and also varies across samples. Which two contributions determine the mean squared error?
choices: Sampling standard deviation and signed bias
Sampling standard deviation and sample size
questions.explanation: Mean squared error reflects variability and the magnitude of the systematic offset.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squared error

questions.clue: When comparing unbiased estimators of the same target, what property identifies the one with the smaller mean squared error?
questions.explanation: For unbiased estimators, only the sampling variance contributes to mean squared error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 149, Efficiency

questions.clue: A scale's estimates have tiny sampling variation but average 5 kg above the target. What does this establish?
questions.explanation: Small variation measures precision, while the average overshoot is positive bias.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 335, Precision

questions.clue: A national survey uses a sample median to estimate national median income. What is the estimand?
choices: The standard error of the median
questions.explanation: The estimand is the population quantity targeted.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimand

questions.clue: An estimation rule returns the same predetermined value for every dataset. What can still prevent the rule from being accurate?
choices: Its estimates can vary greatly across samples
Its standard error can be very large
Its sampled values can be correlated
Its output can have a heavy-tailed distribution
Its constant value can differ from the target
questions.answer: Its constant value can differ from the target
questions.explanation: A constant estimator has no sampling variability but can be biased.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimator

questions.clue: A trial records the sample mean difference between treatment and control. What is the recorded numerical result called?
questions.explanation: The estimate is the realised output of the estimation rule applied to the trial data.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimate

questions.clue: What happens to the expectation of an unbiased estimator if a fixed constant is added to every possible estimate?
choices: It stays at the original target
It shifts by that same constant
It shifts by the square of the constant
It moves in the opposite direction
questions.answer: It shifts by that same constant
questions.explanation: Adding a fixed constant shifts the expectation by that constant.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 440, Unbiased

questions.clue: Estimator Tₙ has bias 1/n and variance 1/n for a fixed target. What happens as n grows?
choices: It is consistent despite finite-sample bias
It is unbiased for every n
questions.answer: It is consistent despite finite-sample bias
questions.explanation: Bias and variance both tend to zero, so MSE tends to zero and the estimator converges in probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Consistency
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{bias}(T_n)=1/n,\quad \mathrm{Var}(T_n)=1/n$
The target is fixed. What happens to this estimator as $n$ grows?

questions.clue: For an infinite sequence of independent draws from a population with positive finite variance, use only the first draw to estimate the mean for every n. How does this rule behave?
questions.explanation: Its expectation is the mean and its variation does not shrink as n grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Consistency
questions.math_clue: For an infinite sequence of independent draws from a population with positive finite variance, use only the first draw to estimate the mean for every $n$. How does this rule behave?

questions.clue: A one-parameter family has an expected value that changes with the parameter. Which feature of a sample does the first-moment method match to that expected value?
questions.explanation: The first raw sample moment is the average of the observations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 277, Method of moments

questions.clue: In a fixed sequence of independent Bernoulli trials, which observed feature is the maximum likelihood estimate of the common success probability?
choices: The chance of observing the most common sequence
The excess of successes over failures
The fraction of trials before the first success
The fraction of trials that succeed
questions.answer: The fraction of trials that succeed
questions.explanation: The likelihood for the common probability is maximized at the observed success fraction.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 273, Maximum likelihood estimation

questions.clue: Among allowed parameter values A, B and C, their likelihoods for the observed data are 0.12, 0.20 and 0.20. Which are maximum likelihood estimates?
questions.explanation: The two largest likelihood values tie.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 273, Maximum likelihood estimation

questions.clue: A survival probability is the complement of event probability. What makes an estimate obtained from the estimated event probability a plug-in estimate?
choices: It evaluates the complement at the estimated event probability
It replaces the event probability by its standard error
It reevaluates the data without the last observation
It assumes the survival probability has maximum likelihood one
It substitutes the observed event times for the sample size
questions.answer: It evaluates the complement at the estimated event probability
questions.explanation: The plug-in principle applies the desired function to an estimate of its argument.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Plug-in principle

questions.clue: For independent Bernoulli trials with fixed n, which summary is sufficient for their common success probability?
choices: Whether the final two outcomes match
The first trial's outcome and the last trial's outcome
questions.explanation: The likelihood depends on the sequence only through its success count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 420, Sufficient statistic

questions.clue: In the usual unbiased sample variance, why is there one fewer residual degree of freedom than observations?
choices: The final observation is omitted from the data
The largest deviation is always discarded
The deviations use a mean estimated from the same sample
A second sample was used to set the mean
The observations must be sampled in pairs
questions.answer: The deviations use a mean estimated from the same sample
questions.explanation: Deviations from the sample mean sum to zero, so one is determined by the others.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue: How does a leave-one-out jackknife construct its replicate datasets?
choices: Split the data into treatment and control
Omit one original observation in turn
Omit every observation with the same outcome
questions.answer: Omit one original observation in turn
questions.explanation: Each jackknife replicate leaves out a different original observation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 226, Jackknife

questions.clue: What does the margin of error represent in a symmetric confidence interval?
choices: The distance from the estimate to either endpoint
The distance from the estimate to zero
The distance from one endpoint to the other
The residual standard deviation of an observation
questions.answer: The distance from the estimate to either endpoint
questions.explanation: The margin of error is the symmetric half-width around the point estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Two symmetric intervals use the same critical multiplier. Which feature gives one a wider margin of error?
choices: A larger point estimate with the same standard error
A smaller point estimate with the same standard error
A change in reporting order for the two endpoints
questions.explanation: The critical multiplier scales the standard error into a margin.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: In the usual symmetric confidence interval, what makes the lower confidence limit the lower of the two endpoints?
choices: The margin of error is added to the estimate
The margin is measured upwards from a sample minimum
The critical multiplier is estimated from the lower half only
The margin of error is subtracted from the estimate
The estimate is divided by the margin of error
questions.answer: The margin of error is subtracted from the estimate
questions.explanation: The lower limit is one margin below the point estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Where is the estimate in a symmetric confidence interval constructed as equal distances around it?
choices: At the midpoint of the interval
At the closest possible value to zero
It can have any location inside the interval
questions.answer: At the midpoint of the interval
questions.explanation: A symmetric interval places its two endpoints at equal distances from the estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Several equal-tail normal intervals target the same parameter using the same estimate and standard error. Which property makes an interval wider?
choices: A different name for the parameter
questions.explanation: A higher confidence level uses a larger critical multiplier when the standard error is fixed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Two comparable mean intervals at 95% are [3, 7] and [1, 9]. Which estimate has greater interval precision?
choices: Precision depends only on the common centre
questions.explanation: The narrower interval reflects a more precise estimate when the methods are comparable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Under a valid 90% confidence procedure, what is expected across many repeated samples?
choices: About 90% of observations are inside each interval
The parameter moves into each interval with probability 90%
About 90% of interval centres equal the parameter
Each interval overlaps 90% of the preceding intervals
About 90% of intervals cover the fixed parameter
questions.answer: About 90% of intervals cover the fixed parameter
questions.explanation: Confidence describes coverage of the method across repeated sampling.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: For a fixed parameter, what varies across repetitions of a valid confidence interval procedure?
choices: The procedure's nominal confidence under its fixed assumptions
questions.explanation: New samples produce new intervals. The target parameter stays fixed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Both endpoints of a two-sided confidence interval for the difference between two means are positive. Which null claim is incompatible with the interval?
choices: The two population means are equal
The first population mean exceeds the second
The true difference could lie inside the interval
questions.answer: The two population means are equal
questions.explanation: Equality corresponds to a difference of zero, which lies outside an interval with two positive endpoints.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: A 95% interval is formed by inverting the corresponding two-sided tests. Its limits are −3 and 2. What does the 5% test do at a null value of zero?
questions.explanation: In an inverted interval, retained values are those the matching test does not reject.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval
questions.math_clue: A 95% interval is formed by inverting the corresponding two-sided tests. Its limits are $-3$ and $2$. What does the 5% test do at a null value of zero?

questions.clue: A 95% confidence interval for a reduction is [1, 4] days. A practical target is at least 5 days. How does the interval compare with that target?
choices: Its lower limit equals the target
The entire interval is above the target
The entire interval is below the target
Its upper limit equals the target
questions.answer: The entire interval is below the target
questions.explanation: Even the upper limit, 4 days, falls below 5.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: Symmetric intervals use a common critical multiplier but have different standard errors. What feature of the intervals will differ because of those standard errors?
choices: The confidence level used for both
The fact that each is symmetric
Which sampling units enter each study
questions.explanation: The width is proportional to the standard error when the multiplier stays fixed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: Why can a larger independent sample make a known-variance mean interval narrower at the same confidence level?
choices: It reduces the population variance by changing the population
It reduces the mean's standard error
It reduces the chosen confidence level
It makes the observed mean equal to zero
It changes a two-sided interval into a one-sided bound
questions.answer: It reduces the mean's standard error
questions.explanation: The standard error of an average decreases with larger independent samples.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: An analysis reports a one-sided 95% lower confidence bound of 8. Which values does the reported confidence set include?
questions.explanation: The confidence set extends upward from its lower boundary.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: An exact 95% upper confidence bound is used repeatedly. In which direction can its bound miss the true parameter?
choices: It can be below the parameter
It misses whenever it is positive
It misses above and below equally often
It can only be above the parameter
questions.answer: It can be below the parameter
questions.explanation: The confidence set extends to smaller values, so a miss occurs if the true parameter exceeds the bound.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: A 95% confidence, 90% coverage tolerance interval is reported. What does the 90% describe?
choices: The fraction of intervals that are symmetric
The chance the population mean is in the realised interval
The targeted fraction of the population covered
questions.answer: The targeted fraction of the population covered
questions.explanation: A tolerance interval targets coverage of individual population values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 432, Tolerance interval

questions.clue: A manufacturer wants limits covering at least 98% of production. Which method directly addresses the fraction of production covered?
choices: A confidence interval for the mean
A confidence interval for the median
An interval for the standard error
A lower bound on the mean
questions.explanation: Tolerance intervals target a specified proportion of the population.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 432, Tolerance interval

questions.clue: In an equal-tail normal confidence interval, how is the probability outside the two critical values divided?
choices: According to the sample mean's sign
questions.explanation: Equal-tail construction splits the excluded probability evenly.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard normal variable

questions.clue: What determines the degrees of freedom for the critical multiplier in a one-sample t interval for a normal population mean?
choices: The observed size of the sample mean
How many different observed values appear
The probability in the upper tail only
The sample size after allowing for the estimated mean
The value of the population's unknown standard deviation
questions.answer: The sample size after allowing for the estimated mean
questions.explanation: The sample mean imposes one constraint on the deviations used to estimate variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student's t-distribution
questions.math_clue: What determines the degrees of freedom for the critical multiplier in a one-sample $t$ interval for a normal population mean?

questions.clue: A scientist changes a mean-distance confidence interval from metres to centimetres. Which feature necessarily stays the same?
choices: The numerical values of the limits
The standard error expressed in the measurement units
questions.explanation: A positive unit conversion changes numerical endpoints and scale while preserving coverage.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: A two-sided confidence interval for a risk ratio is [1.2, 1.8]. Where is its no-difference value?
questions.explanation: Equal risks give a ratio of one, which is below 1.2.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: A preplanned test returns p = 0.03. What happens at significance level 0.05?
choices: Assign the null a probability of 0.03
Retain the null at every alpha
questions.explanation: The p-value is below the stated significance level.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 346, P-value
questions.math_clue: A preplanned test returns $p = 0.03$. What happens at significance level 0.05?

questions.clue: A test gives p = 0.02. Which pair of decisions is correct at levels 0.05 and 0.01, in that order?
choices: Fail to reject, then fail to reject
questions.explanation: The same p-value falls below 0.05 and above 0.01.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 346, P-value
questions.math_clue: A test gives $p = 0.02$. Which pair of decisions is correct at levels 0.05 and 0.01, in that order?

questions.clue: A preplanned study tests only for a decline in defects from a baseline rate of 0.08. What is its alternative?
choices: The defect rate is at least 0.08
questions.explanation: The alternative matches the prespecified direction.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 311, One-sided test

questions.clue: Where is the critical region for a lower one-sided test when small values of the test statistic support the alternative?
choices: In the upper tail of its null distribution
In the lower tail of its null distribution
At both tails with equal probability
In the centre of its null distribution
In both tails with unequal probability
questions.answer: In the lower tail of its null distribution
questions.explanation: Small statistics give evidence in the prespecified direction, so only the lower tail is used.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 115, Critical region

questions.clue: For an observed positive test statistic under a continuous symmetric null law, which region supplies the equal-tail two-sided p-value?
choices: Just the upper tail beyond the statistic
Just the lower tail below the negative of the statistic
Both tails at least as far from zero as the statistic
The middle region between the statistic and its negative
questions.answer: Both tails at least as far from zero as the statistic
questions.explanation: The two-sided test counts equally extreme departures in both directions.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 438, Two-sided test

questions.clue: When a specified alternative is true, which outcome is the complement of rejecting the null?
choices: Rejecting the null when it is true
Failing to reject the null when it is true
questions.explanation: At that alternative, rejection is a detection and non-rejection is a Type II error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: A right-tailed test of a population mean uses a fixed sample size and variance. Which change in the true mean raises its power?
choices: Moving farther above the null mean
Moving toward the null mean from above
Leaving the mean at the null value
Moving farther below the null mean
questions.answer: Moving farther above the null mean
questions.explanation: As the true mean moves in the direction of the alternative, the test statistic is more likely to enter the rejection region.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: For a fixed test statistic and sample size, lowering alpha shrinks a nested rejection region. What happens to power at a fixed alternative?
choices: It can only decrease or stay the same
It can only increase or stay the same
questions.answer: It can only decrease or stay the same
questions.explanation: A smaller rejection region cannot increase the chance of falling inside it.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: When the null is true, which long-run outcome does the Type I error rate describe?
choices: The fraction of tests that fail to reject the null
The fraction of tests that detect a real effect
The size of the estimated effect
The standard deviation of the null distribution
The fraction of tests that reject the null
questions.answer: The fraction of tests that reject the null
questions.explanation: A rejection is a false positive whenever the tested null is true.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error

questions.clue: A quality check flags a correctly calibrated instrument as miscalibrated. With correct calibration as the null, what happened?
questions.explanation: The test rejected a null that was true.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error

questions.clue: Which change usually raises power for a fixed nonzero effect in a normal mean test at a fixed significance level?
choices: Move the true effect closer to zero
Reduce both sample size and effect magnitude
questions.explanation: More independent observations reduce the mean's standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: For fixed familywise significance, what happens to the common Bonferroni cutoff as the number of hypotheses increases?
choices: It becomes the smallest observed p-value
It becomes unrelated to the familywise level
questions.explanation: The allowed familywise level is divided among more individual tests.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bonferroni correction

questions.clue: What event defines familywise error when all four nulls in a family are true?
choices: At least one null is rejected
questions.answer: At least one null is rejected
questions.explanation: Familywise error counts the occurrence of one or more false rejections.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 164, Familywise error rate

questions.clue: For a randomized two-group trial under a sharp no-effect null, what is changed when recalculating the statistic in each permutation?
choices: Treatment labels under the original assignment scheme
questions.answer: Treatment labels under the original assignment scheme
questions.explanation: The sharp null keeps each outcome fixed under reassignment, so treatment labels vary according to the design.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Permutation test

questions.clue: In the ordinary paired sign test, which observations are removed before assigning positive or negative signs?
choices: Pairs with the largest absolute difference
Pairs with equal signs as their neighbours
questions.explanation: A zero difference has neither a positive nor a negative sign and is treated as a tie.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 393, Sign test

questions.clue: A team recruits volunteers and assigns each by a coin toss to one of two programs. Which random step occurred?
questions.explanation: The coin toss allocates treatments among enrolled people.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random allocation

questions.clue: Families choose their own meal plans, and investigators compare health later without assigning any plan. What type of study is this?
questions.explanation: The researchers measure outcomes after participants choose their own exposure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 308, Observational study

questions.clue: An examiner scores injuries without seeing treatment assignments. Whose blinding does this establish?
questions.explanation: The examiner measures outcomes without knowing the groups.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 57, Blinding

questions.clue: An inactive pill matches an experimental medication in appearance. Which trial feature does the inactive pill provide?
questions.explanation: A matched inactive pill helps control for the experience and expectations of receiving medication.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Placebo

questions.clue: A team measures current symptoms and current work hours in one survey. Which design best describes its time structure?
questions.explanation: Exposure and outcome are measured at a common point or short period.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Cross-sectional study

questions.clue: A case-control study deliberately recruits 100 patients with a condition and 100 controls. Which quantity did the recruitment rule fix at 50% in the data?
choices: The sample fraction with the condition
questions.answer: The sample fraction with the condition
questions.explanation: The design fixes the disease split in the sample, so the split does not estimate prevalence.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 69, Case-control study

questions.clue: Researchers select current welders and office workers, then track future breathing problems. Which design follows these exposure groups?
questions.explanation: The exposures define the groups, and outcomes are measured later.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 90, Cohort study

questions.clue: A trial randomizes separately within each hospital. For that randomization, what role does hospital play?
questions.explanation: Patients are grouped by site before treatment allocation within each group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: What does it mean for a diet and exercise study to use a full factorial design?
choices: It includes every combination of diet and exercise levels
It includes diets paired only with their most common exercise plan
It tests all diets but uses only one exercise level
It tests all exercise levels but uses only one diet
It assigns both factors but never in the same group
questions.answer: It includes every combination of diet and exercise levels
questions.explanation: A full factorial crosses each level of one factor with every level of the other.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Each participant receives both devices in separate periods. Which comparison uses this crossover design to control stable differences among participants?
choices: Compare only each person's first response with the population mean
Compare different people who received the same device
Compare the two periods without regard to device
Compare group sizes across the two sequences
Compare each person's responses on the two devices
questions.answer: Compare each person's responses on the two devices
questions.explanation: Each person serves as their own comparison across devices.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Crossover design

questions.clue: A treatment has effects lasting days. What design component reduces contamination of the next treatment period?
choices: A new random seed for analysis
questions.explanation: An interval between treatments allows the earlier effect to dissipate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 453, Wash-out period

questions.clue: A participant assigned to control switches to active treatment. In an intention-to-treat analysis, to which group does the participant contribute?
questions.explanation: Intention-to-treat retains the original randomized assignment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Intention-to-treat analysis

questions.clue: An analysis includes only participants who met the adherence rules in their assigned arms. What defines its analysis set?
choices: The direction of the estimated effect
questions.explanation: A per-protocol set is restricted to participants satisfying protocol criteria.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Per protocol
